# 

# 1\. LAB OVERVIEW

## 1.1  Why This Lab Exists

Real outages leave evidence in several places: the web tier reports the errors, the application logs show the struggle, the operating system records the kill, and the database may show unrelated noise. An investigation must combine indexes, sourcetypes and hosts into one timeline, find where an error spike really comes from, zoom into the critical minutes, and relate everything to the service view that managers see in ITSI.  
In this lab you investigate INC-9120 end to end: a timeline across four indexes, error spikes by host and sourcetype (and why the hosts that log the errors are not the broken ones), tightly time-bound searches around the out-of-memory kill, and the ITSI KPI and service health data for the same hour, read the way you would read a KPI dashboard and a glass table.

| 🎯  NIIT iRUN Alignment |
| :---- |
| INCIDENT OWNERSHIP: You can build the evidence-based timeline of an outage from several indexes. |
|  |
| TROUBLESHOOTING EXCELLENCE: You will distinguish where an error is reported from where it originates. |
|  |
| OPERATIONAL READINESS: You can explain a service health score drop with the KPI that caused it. |

## 1.3  Conceptual Foundation

Advanced investigation is mostly about combining sources correctly and choosing the right time window.  
*Figure: Multi-Index Investigation — Web (Symptom: 502\) ← App (Struggle: GC, OOM) ← OS (Kill, Restart) · DB (Unrelated Noise) → One Timeline → Service View (ITSI KPIs, Health Score, Glass Table)*

| Metadata Field | Set At | Use In Investigation | Example |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| index | Ingestion (where data is stored) | Choose the data sources; access control | d3\_web, d3\_app, d3\_infra, d3\_db |
| sourcetype | Ingestion (format of the data) | Select the parser/fields; compare log types | access\_combined, \_json, syslog |
| host | Ingestion (who sent/produced the event) | Find the machine that logged or produced it | web-01 logs a 502 caused by app-02 |
| \_time | Parsed from the event | Time-bound searches and timelines | earliest="10/22/2026:10:30:00" |

*Figure: ITSI Views — KPI (Base Search, Thresholds) → Service Health Score (Weighted by Importance) → Service Tree (Dependencies) → Service Analyzer / Glass Table (Business View Coloured by Severity)*

## 1.4  Learning Objectives

* Investigate a service outage using multiple indexes and build one timeline  
* Investigate error spikes using host and sourcetype  
* Separate the host that reports an error from the host that causes it  
* Use precise time-bound searches to analyse the critical minutes  
* Read ITSI KPI and service health data and explain a health score drop  
* Interpret a glass table view and identify false alarms

## 1.5  What You Will NOT Do

| 🚫  Hard Stops — Absolute Prohibitions for This Lab |
| :---- |
| ✗  NEVER search index=\* over long time ranges during an incident — name the indexes |
| ✗  NEVER blame the host that logged the error without checking where the request went |
| ✗  NEVER change ITSI thresholds during an incident to make a dashboard green |
| ✗  NEVER share raw events with customer data outside the incident channel |
| ✗  NEVER treat every red KPI as an incident — check user impact first |

# 

# 3\. CONCEPT DEEP-DIVE BEFORE STARTING

## 3.1  Investigating Across Indexes

Each index holds one kind of evidence, and each sourcetype has its own fields — status in access logs, level in JSON application logs, free text in syslog. A multi-index search retrieves all relevant indexes at once, uses OR between the conditions that matter in each source, and normalises them with eval (for example a "signal" field) so that stats can build one timeline. host tells you who wrote the event, which is not always where the problem is.

| 💡  Why This Matters Operationally |
| :---- |
| The quickest way to end a blame discussion is a single timeline with every source in it. |
|  |
| ITSI turns the same searches into KPIs and health scores; knowing the KPI behind a red tile tells you which search to open. |

## 3.2  The Critical Distinction: Reporting Host vs Failing Host

In a layered system the component closest to the user reports the error. nginx on web-01 and web-02 logged every 502, so a "count by host" makes the web servers look guilty. The upstream field shows that every failed request went to app-02, and app-02's own logs and syslog show why. Always follow the request path from the reporting host to the component that actually failed.

| ⚠️  Most Common Mistake in Multi-Source Investigations |
| :---- |
| An engineer sees the database slow-query warnings in the timeline and declares "the database was slow" — the DBA disagrees, and the meeting ends without a root cause. |
|  |
| REASON: The slow queries happened at 10:10, twenty minutes before the outage, with no effect on response times; they are noise in the same hour. |
|  |
| YOU MUST check that a candidate cause happens before AND close to the symptoms, explains their mechanism, and that the symptoms stop when it stops. |

## 3.3  Time-Bound Search Options

| Technique | Syntax | Use | Note |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Absolute window | earliest="10/22/2026:10:30:00" latest="10/22/2026:10:32:00" | Historic incidents | Format %m/%d/%Y:%H:%M:%S |
| Relative window | earliest=-15m@m latest=@m | Live incidents | Relative to now; @m snaps to the minute |
| Time picker | Date & Time Range / Advanced | Interactive zoom | Click-drag on the timeline zooms in |
| Event time filter | \| where \_time \>= strptime("…", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S") | Inside a pipeline | Slower than retrieval-time limits |

| 📝  How to Decide Whether a Signal Belongs to the Incident |
| :---- |
| Ask: "Did it start shortly before the symptoms, does it explain how the symptoms happen, and did it stop when they stopped?" GC warnings on app-02 (from 10:24), the OOM kill (10:30:58) and the restart (10:37:20) pass all three tests. The database slow queries (10:10–10:11) and the routine payment declines fail them. |

| **1.A  Write the incident timeline in five lines (time — event — host — source).**  Answer:  10:24 – GC pause warnings begin – app-02 – Application logs. 10:30:58 – Out-of-memory kill – app-02 – System logs. 10:31:00–10:37:18 – HTTP 502 errors – web-01 and web-02 – Web access logs. 10:37:15 – Shop API restart begins – app-02 – System logs. 10:37:20 – Shop API successfully restarts – app-02 – System logs.  |
| **1.B  Which rows are noise (not part of the incident) and why? Use the three questions from the concept section.**  Answer: The database slow queries at 10:10–10:11 are unrelated because they occurred well before the outage and did not cause the web response-time degradation. Routine payment declines are also noise because they do not explain the app-02 GC warnings, OOM kill or subsequent 502 errors. |

Error spikes are first seen per host and sourcetype. You chart errors per minute by host, break them down by sourcetype, enrich hosts with their role and data centre, and then follow the upstream field to the host that actually failed.

| **2.A  Both web hosts (in two data centres) show the spike. Why does that rule out a web-server problem?**  Answer: Both web servers, located in separate data centres, reported errors at the same time. The upstream field shows that all 85 failed requests were sent to app-02. Therefore, the problem originated in the shared backend application server rather than the individual web servers.  |
| **2.B  The app-03 ERROR at 10:30:07 appears in the spike chart. Is it related? Prove it with one search.**  Answer: No. The app-03 error is unrelated to the outage because the main failure evidence points to app-02. The app-03 error is an isolated event and does not explain the 502 errors routed to app-02. Use this search to inspect the app-03 event: index=d3\_app host=app-03 earliest="10/22/2026:04:30:00" latest="10/22/2026:05:30:00" level=ERROR \| table \_time host level msg |

Time-bound searches narrow the evidence to the minutes that matter: what happened on app-02 just before, during and after the kill, how much evidence exists in a two-minute window, and when app-02 stopped and resumed processing requests.

| ⌨  Task 3 — Narrow windows |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# Step 1: The operating system view of app-02 (no cron noise) |
| index=d3\_infra host=app-02 earliest="10/22/2026:10:30:50" latest="10/22/2026:10:38:00" NOT CRON \| table \_time \_raw |
|  |
| \# Step 2: Everything in the two minutes around the kill, by index |
| index=d3\_\* earliest="10/22/2026:10:30:00" latest="10/22/2026:10:32:00" \| stats count by index |

| index=d3\_app host=app-02 earliest="10/22/2026:10:29:00" latest="10/22/2026:10:40:00" \| timechart span=1m count |
|  |
| \# Step 4: Relative time modifiers (for live incidents) — explain what each returns now |
| index=d3\_web earliest=-15m@m latest=@m \| stats count |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Step 1: 10:30:58 kernel: … Out of memory: Killed process 2211 (java) … · 10:30:59 Main process exited, code=killed, status=9/KILL |
|         10:30:59 Failed with result 'oom-kill'. · 10:31:04 Scheduled restart job … · 10:31:04 Start request repeated too quickly. |
|         10:37:15 Starting shop-api.service … · 10:37:20 Started shop-api.service \- Shop API.![][image8] |
| Step 2: d3\_app 136 · d3\_db 1 · d3\_infra 9 · d3\_web 80![][image9] |
| Step 3: 10:29 28 · 10:30 29 · 10:31–10:36 0 · 10:37 18 · 10:38 27 · 10:39 26![][image10] |
| Step 4: 0 — the data is from 22 Oct 2026, so a window relative to now is empty![][image11] |
| **3.A  How long was app-02 unavailable, and why did the first restart attempt fail ("Start request repeated too quickly")?**  Answer: App-02 was unavailable from approximately 10:30:58 until 10:37:20, around 6 minutes and 22 seconds. The first restart attempt failed because the service manager detected repeated rapid failures and triggered its start-rate limit after the out-of-memory kill.   |
| **3.B  Explain earliest=-15m@m latest=@m. When would you use it instead of an absolute window?**  Answer: `earliest=-15m@m` searches from 15 minutes ago, rounded down to the minute. `latest=@m` searches up to the current minute. It is useful for monitoring live incidents, whereas absolute timestamps are preferable for investigating historical incidents. |

|         10:10  40        40           100       100 |
|         10:20  100       75           90        75 |
|         10:25  100       62           70        62 |
|         10:30  100       23           30        23 |
|         10:35  100       40           40        48      (all other rows 100\) ![][image12] |
| Step 2: 10:10 Database Slow queries 6 high · 10:20 Shop Web p95 1.206 high · 10:20 Shop API GC 2 medium |
|         10:25 Shop Web p95 2.315 critical · 10:25 Shop API GC 10 critical · 10:30 Shop Web 5xx 27.0 critical · p95 1.365 high |
|         10:30 Shop API Instances 66.7 critical · GC 2 medium · 10:35 Shop Web 5xx 15.5 critical · Shop API Instances 66.7 critical![][image13] |
| Step 3: Database Slow queries 6 high; all Shop Web and Shop API KPIs normal![][image14] |
| **4.A  Explain both drops of Online Shop health (10:10 and 10:25–10:35): which KPI, which service, real user impact or not?**  Answer: The first drop at 10:10 was caused by high database slow queries. However, the Shop Web and Shop API KPIs remained normal, indicating that it was an isolated database issue without significant customer-facing impact. The second drop between 10:25 and 10:35 was a genuine application outage. Shop Web experienced increased response time and HTTP 5xx errors, while Shop API showed GC pause warnings and reduced instance availability. These issues were associated with the app-02 failure and resulted in HTTP 502 errors. |
| **4.B  The "worst child" rule made Online Shop red at 10:10. How would KPI importance or dependency weighting in ITSI avoid this false alarm?**  Answer: KPI importance and service dependencies help ensure that service health reflects actual business impact. Customer-facing services and critical KPIs should receive greater weight, while isolated issues with low-impact dependencies should not unnecessarily make the entire application appear unhealthy. This reduces false alarms and provides a more accurate representation of service health. |

| **V6: Did you explain both health drops correctly?**  Answer: Yes. The 10:10 health drop was caused by isolated database slow queries without user impact. The 10:25–10:35 health deterioration represented the actual incident, with Shop Web errors and latency increases and Shop API availability and GC issues. |

# 6\. TROUBLESHOOTING — COMMON ISSUES & FIXES

| Issue / Error | Cause | Diagnosis | Fix |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| case() returns null signal | Index names differ (e.g. typo) or quotes wrong | stats count by index | Use index=="d3\_web" with double equals inside eval |
| Timechart by host shows "OTHER" | More than 10 hosts in the result | Add limit=0 | \| timechart span=1m limit=0 count by host |
| Syslog events at wrong times | Timestamp parsed without the offset | Compare \_time with the raw ISO time | Keep the ISO timestamps with \+05:30; reload if edited |
| NOT CRON removes too much | Term matches inside other words | Run without NOT CRON | Use NOT "CRON\[" or a field filter |
| inputlookup returns nothing | CSV missing from the lookups folder | ls \$SPLUNK\_HOME/etc/apps/search/lookups | Copy itsi\_\*.csv again (Lab 1 load script) |
| xyseries columns in unexpected order | Alphabetical column order | Check the header | Add \| table time "Online Shop" "Shop Web" "Shop API" Database |

# 7\. INSTRUCTOR DEBRIEF — 7 MINUTES

## 7.1  Discussion Questions

| Discussion 1 — Ending the Blame Game |
| :---- |
| Without notes: use the timeline to answer the web team and the DBA in one sentence each. |
| Which single search convinced you most? |
|  |
| Key answer to explore: the upstream breakdown — every 502 went to app-02, whose OOM kill explains the outage. |
| **Discussion 2 — Host and Sourcetype** |
| Why did "count by host" point at the wrong servers? |
| What extra field should every layer log to make the request path visible? |
|  |
| Key insight: the reporting host is the edge; upstream/backend or trace IDs reveal the failing component. |
| **Discussion 3 — Time Windows** |
| When are absolute windows better than relative ones? |
| How narrow should a window be when you share a search in an incident channel? |
|  |
| Key answer: absolute for history and sharing (reproducible); relative for live dashboards and alerts. |
| **Discussion 4 — ITSI Health Scores** |
| What did the KPI view tell you that the health score alone did not? |
| How should KPI importance be chosen? |
|  |
| Answer: the KPI and its value explain the colour; importance must reflect user and business impact, so noise KPIs do not turn the business service red. |

## 7.2  Common Mistakes — Learn From These

| Mistake | Why It Happens | Consequence | Prevention |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Blaming the reporting host | It logged the errors | Wrong team, longer outage | Follow upstream/backend fields |
| Accepting every signal in the window | Proximity bias | False root causes | Before \+ close \+ mechanism \+ stops with symptoms |
| Relative windows on historic data | Habit from live work | Empty results | Absolute earliest/latest |
| Reading only health colours | Dashboards are colourful | Cause unknown | Open the KPI behind the tile |
| Index=\* searches | Not knowing where data lives | Slow, costly searches | Name the indexes; keep a data map |

# 10\. QUICK REFERENCE — ADVANCED SPLUNK INVESTIGATION COMMAND CARD

Bookmark this page. Every command you need in SOP order.

| Category | Command | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Several indexes | index=d3\_\* (cond1 OR cond2 …) | One search |
| Normalise | \| eval signal=case(index=="a", …, index=="b", …) | Common label |
| Timeline | \| stats min(\_time) max(\_time) count by signal, host | First / last |
| Per host | \| timechart span=1m limit=0 count by host | Spikes |
| Per sourcetype | \| stats count by sourcetype, host | Which log type |
| Request path | \| rex "upstream=(?\<backend\>…)" \| stats count by host, backend | Failing host |
| Absolute time | earliest="10/22/2026:10:30:00" latest="…" | Historic |
| Relative time | earliest=-15m@m latest=@m | Live |
| Exclude noise | NOT CRON | Narrow results |
| ITSI health | \| inputlookup itsi\_health.csv \| xyseries time service health\_score | Service Analyzer view |
| ITSI KPIs | \| inputlookup itsi\_kpis.csv \| where severity\!="normal" | Why it is red |
| Owner | \| lookup service\_owners.csv service OUTPUT oncall | Escalation |
